questions.stem: Which two structures make up the central nervous system?
options: The somatic and autonomic systems
The brain and the spinal cord
The brain and the cranial nerves
The spinal cord and the spinal nerves
questions.explanation: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The cranial and spinal nerves branch out from it and belong to the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: The peripheral nervous system is best described as:
options: the part of the brain that controls involuntary actions
all the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord
the nerve fibres that link the brain to the spinal cord
the interneurons inside the spinal cord
questions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system is every part of the nervous system outside the brain and spinal cord. Fibres linking the brain and spinal cord are inside the central nervous system.

questions.stem: The somatic nervous system and the autonomic nervous system are both divisions of the:
options: sympathetic nervous system
parasympathetic nervous system
peripheral nervous system
central nervous system
questions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system divides into the somatic and autonomic nervous systems. The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions sit one level lower, inside the autonomic nervous system.

questions.stem: Which describes a main role of the spinal cord?
options: Storing long-term memories of motor skills such as riding a bike
Producing the hormones that trigger the fight-flight response
Interpreting visual information received from the eyes
Relaying messages between the brain and the peripheral nervous system
questions.explanation: The spinal cord carries sensory messages up to the brain and motor messages down to the peripheral nervous system. Interpreting vision is done by the visual cortex in the brain, not the spinal cord.

questions.stem: A rider's spinal cord is badly damaged at waist level in a fall. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Loss of sensation and voluntary movement below the injury
Loss of sensation above the injury but normal movement below it
Loss of hearing and of the ability to understand speech
Loss of the ability to form new memories of events
questions.explanation: The spinal cord carries sensory messages up and motor messages down, so damage cuts off both for body parts below the injury. Hearing, language and memory depend on the brain, which is above the injury.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the somatic nervous system?
options: Releasing hormones into the bloodstream to regulate the body
Carrying sensory messages to the CNS and motor messages to skeletal muscles
Controlling heart rate, digestion and other involuntary organ activity
Relaying messages between the two hemispheres of the brain
questions.explanation: The somatic nervous system has a sensory division carrying information from receptors to the central nervous system and a motor division carrying messages to skeletal muscles. Control of organs such as the heart is the autonomic nervous system's role.

questions.stem: Jai decides to kick a football. Which division carries the message from his central nervous system to his leg muscles?
options: The parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
The motor division of the somatic nervous system
The sensory division of the somatic nervous system
The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: Voluntary movement of skeletal muscles is controlled by the motor division of the somatic nervous system. The sensory division carries messages the other way, from receptors towards the central nervous system.

questions.stem: Walking barefoot on the beach, Amira notices the sand is hot. Which division carried this information to her central nervous system?
options: The sensory division of the somatic nervous system
The motor division of the somatic nervous system
The parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: Information from receptors in the skin travels to the central nervous system along the sensory division of the somatic nervous system. The motor division carries messages out to the muscles, not in from the skin.

questions.stem: In the somatic nervous system, sensory neurons are also called ___ neurons and motor neurons are also called ___ neurons.
options: afferent; efferent
efferent; afferent
excitatory; inhibitory
presynaptic; postsynaptic
questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) neurons carry messages towards the central nervous system and efferent (motor) neurons carry messages away from it. Excitatory and inhibitory describe the effects of neurotransmitters, not types of neuron.

questions.stem: Which activity is controlled by the somatic rather than the autonomic nervous system?
options: Your stomach churning as it digests lunch
Turning your head towards a friend who calls your name
Sweating on a hot afternoon
Pupils widening as you walk into a dark room
questions.explanation: Turning the head is a voluntary movement of skeletal muscles, so it uses the somatic nervous system. Sweating, pupil size and digestion involve glands and visceral muscles, which the autonomic nervous system controls.

questions.stem: Which division of the nervous system regulates the heart, glands and digestive organs, largely without conscious control?
options: The central nervous system
The sensory (afferent) division
The autonomic nervous system
The somatic nervous system
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system connects the central nervous system to visceral muscles, organs and glands and works largely without conscious control. The somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the sympathetic nervous system?
options: Arousing the body to respond to a threat or emergency
Returning the body to a calm state once a threat has passed
Carrying voluntary movement commands to skeletal muscles
Relaying sensory information from the skin to the spinal cord
questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action, the fight-flight response, when a threat is perceived. Calming the body once the threat has passed is the role of the parasympathetic nervous system.

questions.stem: Which pair of changes is produced by activation of the sympathetic nervous system?
options: Heart rate slows and saliva increases
Breathing slows and the bladder contracts
Pupils dilate and digestion slows
Pupils constrict and digestion speeds up
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation dilates the pupils and slows digestion, while increasing heart rate and breathing. Constricted pupils, faster digestion, a slower heart and more saliva are all parasympathetic effects.

questions.stem: Why does the sympathetic nervous system slow digestion when a person faces a threat?
options: Digestion would release hormones that block the neurotransmitters
The muscles of the stomach are controlled by the somatic system
Slowing digestion lowers the heart rate so the body stays calm
Energy and blood flow are redirected to the muscles needed for action
questions.explanation: During the fight-flight response, non-essential functions such as digestion are slowed so that energy and blood can go to the skeletal muscles. Lowering heart rate is a parasympathetic effect and would not help a person deal with a threat.

questions.stem: The parasympathetic nervous system mainly:
options: maintains the body's normal functioning and calms it after arousal
prepares the body for action when a threat is perceived
carries sensory messages from receptors to the brain
sends voluntary motor commands to the skeletal muscles
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system keeps the body's organs working at their usual level and returns the body to that state after sympathetic arousal. Preparing for action is the role of the sympathetic nervous system.

questions.stem: After a near-miss in traffic, Ella's racing heart gradually slows and her digestion resumes. Which division is now dominant?
options: The sympathetic nervous system
The motor division of the somatic nervous system
The sensory division of the somatic nervous system
The parasympathetic nervous system
questions.explanation: Slowing the heart and restarting digestion are signs that the parasympathetic nervous system has become dominant again, restoring the body's normal functioning. The sympathetic nervous system caused the racing heart in the first place.

questions.stem: Which statement about the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems is correct?
options: Both are active at the same time, with one usually dominant
Only one of them can be active at any given moment
The parasympathetic system is part of the somatic system
The sympathetic system carries sensory messages to the brain
questions.explanation: The two divisions work together continuously, and whichever one is dominant depends on the situation. They do not switch on and off completely, and both belong to the autonomic nervous system.

questions.stem: A hiker sees a snake on the track. Her heart pounds, and she steps backwards. Which divisions produce the stepping back and the pounding heart, in that order?
options: Somatic sensory division; parasympathetic division
Somatic motor division; sympathetic division
Sympathetic division; somatic motor division
Parasympathetic division; sympathetic division
questions.explanation: Stepping backwards is voluntary movement of skeletal muscles, produced by the somatic motor division. The pounding heart is part of the fight-flight response produced by the sympathetic division.

questions.stem: A student claims the autonomic nervous system is completely involuntary and can never be influenced by conscious effort. Which observation best challenges this?
options: Sensory neurons carry messages from the organs to the brain
People can deliberately slow their breathing, which lowers their heart rate
People can choose to move their arms whenever they wish
Spinal reflexes happen before the brain is aware of the stimulus
questions.explanation: Slowing the breath on purpose can reduce heart rate, showing that autonomic functions can be influenced consciously to some degree. Moving the arms is somatic control, so it says nothing about the autonomic nervous system.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the dendrites?
options: Insulating the axon to speed up transmission
Releasing neurotransmitters into the synapse
Carrying the message away from the soma
Receiving messages from other neurons
questions.explanation: Dendrites are branch-like fibres that receive messages from neighbouring neurons and pass them to the soma. Releasing neurotransmitter is the job of the axon terminals.

questions.stem: The soma (cell body) of a neuron:
options: insulates the axon so that messages travel faster
releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic gap
is the junction where two neurons communicate
contains the nucleus and combines the incoming signals
questions.explanation: The soma contains the nucleus, keeps the neuron alive and combines the signals received by the dendrites. Insulating the axon is the role of the myelin sheath.

questions.stem: At the same moment, a neuron receives excitatory neurotransmitter at some synapses and inhibitory neurotransmitter at others. What determines whether it fires?
options: The thickness of the myelin sheath covering its dendrites
Whether the message is heading towards or away from the brain
The overall balance of excitatory and inhibitory input it receives
Whichever neurotransmitter happened to reach the neuron first
questions.explanation: A neuron combines all its inputs, and it fires only if the excitatory input outweighs the inhibitory input strongly enough. Myelin covers axons rather than dendrites, and the order of arrival does not decide the outcome on its own.

questions.stem: The myelin sheath:
options: contains the nucleus and keeps the neuron alive
stores neurotransmitters in tiny sacs
insulates the axon and speeds up transmission
receives chemical messages from other neurons
questions.explanation: Myelin is a fatty coating on many axons that insulates them and allows messages to travel much faster. Neurotransmitters are stored in vesicles in the axon terminals, not in the myelin.

questions.stem: What do the axon terminals do?
options: Release neurotransmitters into the synaptic gap
Receive neurotransmitters from the previous neuron
Produce the myelin that coats the axon
Hold the nucleus and control the cell
questions.explanation: Axon terminals at the end of the axon contain neurotransmitter that is released into the synaptic gap when a message arrives. Receiving neurotransmitter happens at the dendrites of the next neuron.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the direction a neural message travels through a single neuron?
options: Axon terminals, axon, soma, dendrites
Soma, dendrites, axon, axon terminals
Dendrites, axon, soma, axon terminals
Dendrites, soma, axon, axon terminals
questions.explanation: A message is received by the dendrites, passed to the soma, carried along the axon and released at the axon terminals. Transmission within a neuron runs in this one direction.

questions.stem: In multiple sclerosis, the myelin sheath on axons is damaged. Which effect would you expect?
options: Dendrites can no longer receive any incoming messages
Messages begin to travel backwards along the axon
Messages travel along affected axons more slowly or erratically
Neurotransmitter can no longer be made anywhere in the neuron
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon and speeds transmission, so losing it slows or disrupts messages. The dendrites and the direction of transmission are not what myelin controls.

questions.stem: Sensory neurons carry information:
options: from sensory receptors towards the central nervous system
from the central nervous system out to the muscles
between other neurons inside the brain and spinal cord
from the brain to glands that release hormones
questions.explanation: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry information from receptors in the body towards the central nervous system. Carrying messages out to muscles is the job of motor neurons.

questions.stem: Where are interneurons found, and what do they do?
options: In skeletal muscles, triggering them to contract
In the glands, controlling hormone release
In the CNS, linking sensory and motor neurons
In the skin, detecting touch and temperature
questions.explanation: Interneurons are found only in the brain and spinal cord, where they connect sensory and motor neurons and carry messages between other neurons. Detecting stimuli is done by sensory receptors.

questions.stem: Which type of neuron is by far the most numerous in the human nervous system?
options: Autonomic neurons
Interneurons
Sensory neurons
Motor neurons
questions.explanation: Interneurons make up the great majority of neurons because the brain and spinal cord are made mostly of them. Sensory and motor neurons are far fewer.

questions.stem: Ravi's finger muscles contract as he grips a pen. Which neurons carried the message that caused the contraction?
options: Sensory (afferent) neurons
Interneurons in the fingers
Parasympathetic neurons
Motor (efferent) neurons
questions.explanation: Motor neurons carry messages from the central nervous system to muscles, causing them to contract. Interneurons are found only in the central nervous system, not in the fingers.

questions.stem: Lena touches a cactus spine and pulls her hand back before she feels any pain. Which neurons carry the message, in order?
options: Motor neuron, interneuron in the spinal cord, sensory neuron
Sensory neuron, interneuron in the cortex, motor neuron
Interneuron in the spinal cord, sensory neuron, motor neuron
Sensory neuron, interneuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron
questions.explanation: The sensory neuron carries the message to the spinal cord, an interneuron there passes it on, and a motor neuron makes the arm muscle contract. Because the loop runs through the spinal cord, the hand moves before the message reaches the brain and pain is felt.

questions.stem: After an injury, a man can feel a light touch on his left foot but cannot move the foot voluntarily. Damage is most likely to the:
options: sympathetic neurons serving the left leg
motor neurons serving the left foot
sensory neurons serving the left foot
parasympathetic neurons serving the left leg
questions.explanation: Feeling touch shows the sensory neurons are working, so the loss of voluntary movement points to motor neurons. The sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons control glands and organs, not voluntary movement.

questions.stem: Neural transmission is described as electro-chemical because messages travel:
options: chemically within a neuron and electrically between neurons
electrically in the brain and chemically in the spinal cord
electrically in sensory neurons and chemically in motor neurons
electrically within a neuron and chemically between neurons
questions.explanation: A message travels along a neuron as an electrical impulse and crosses the synapse to the next neuron as a chemical, the neurotransmitter. The reversed version mixes up the two stages.

questions.stem: The synapse is best described as:
options: the site where an axon terminal meets a receiving neuron across a tiny gap
the fatty layer that insulates an axon and speeds transmission
the part of the soma where incoming messages are combined
the bundle of fibres that joins the two hemispheres
questions.explanation: The synapse is the point of communication between neurons, made up of the axon terminal, the synaptic gap and the receptor sites of the receiving neuron. The fatty insulating layer is the myelin sheath.

questions.stem: What happens when an electrical impulse reaches the axon terminals?
options: Neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic gap
The myelin sheath sends an electrical charge across the gap
The dendrites of the same neuron fire back towards the soma
The soma produces a fresh impulse at the terminals
questions.explanation: The arriving impulse causes the axon terminals to release neurotransmitter, which crosses the synaptic gap to the next neuron. The electrical impulse itself does not jump the gap.

questions.stem: Neurotransmitter affects a receiving neuron by:
options: travelling along its axon to the terminals
attaching to the outside of its myelin sheath
entering its nucleus and changing its DNA
binding to receptor sites on its dendrites
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic gap and binds to matching receptor sites on the receiving neuron, usually on its dendrites. It does not travel along the axon or change the neuron's DNA.

questions.stem: Glutamate is an excitatory neurotransmitter. When it binds to a receiving neuron, that neuron becomes:
options: unable to receive messages
unable to release neurotransmitter
more likely to fire
less likely to fire
questions.explanation: An excitatory neurotransmitter such as glutamate makes the receiving neuron more likely to fire. An inhibitory neurotransmitter such as GABA has the opposite effect.

questions.stem: Why can a neural message cross a synapse in only one direction?
options: The myelin sheath blocks any message travelling back towards the soma
Dendrites release neurotransmitter, but axon terminals cannot detect it
Electrical charge in the synaptic gap repels messages going backwards
Neurotransmitter is released only from axon terminals and received only at receptor sites
questions.explanation: Only the axon terminals of the sending neuron release neurotransmitter, and only the receiving neuron has the matching receptor sites, so transmission runs one way. Dendrites receive rather than release neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the receptor sites for an excitatory neurotransmitter on receiving neurons. What is the most likely effect?
options: Messages start travelling backwards across the synapse
The receiving neurons fire less often
The receiving neurons fire more often
More neurotransmitter is made in the dendrites
questions.explanation: If the excitatory neurotransmitter cannot bind, the receiving neurons lose the input that would make them more likely to fire, so they fire less. Blocking receptors does not reverse the direction of transmission.
